idiom_name: final public method + abstract/overridable hook in an abstract class or trait
implementation_notes: Scala methods are virtual by default, so the non-virtual half is written with `final` - a final member may not be overridden (Scala spec, Classes & Objects) - while the hook stays abstract or simply non-final. Traits carry the wrapper and the abstract hooks and the concrete class supplies them; `abstract override` lets a stackable trait wrap a hook that is implemented further down the linearization (the SynchronizedTable get/set example in the spec). `final` cannot be combined with `abstract` (error E060), so keep the wrapper and the hooks in separate members and mark hooks `protected` to keep them out of the client API.
code_sketch:
abstract class Saveable:
  final def save(): Unit =          // cannot be overridden
    lock.synchronized(coreSave())

  protected def coreSave(): Unit

final class Customer extends Saveable:
  protected def coreSave(): Unit = { /* ... */ }
pitfalls: Without `final` the wrapper is virtual again; a subclass may also widen a protected hook to public on override (visibility can only be widened, never narrowed).
Trait linearization decides which `super` implementation an abstract override hook wraps; a stackable trait that calls super before an implementation exists fails only at the mixin site.
`final` may not be combined with `abstract` (E060) - do not try to make the wrapper abstract; the hook is the abstract member.
